passages.t: Paul to Timothy, his true child in the faith
passages.happening: “Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the command of God our Savior and of Christ Jesus our hope, To Timothy, my true child in the faith: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord” (verses 1-2).
passages.hearers:
This is a letter to one person, but it was surely meant to be heard by the church too. That is why Paul begins with his authority: ‘an apostle … by the command of God’. Timothy would need it. He had to correct people who were older than he was, and some of them were the church's own teachers. When Timothy spoke, he was not speaking for himself.

Notice the names Paul gives. God is ‘our Savior’, a title the letter will use again and again. Christ Jesus is ‘our hope’. In a city full of gods who promised protection, Paul says there is one Saviour and one hope.

Then comes the warmth. Timothy is ‘my true child in the faith’. They were not related. But Paul had led him on in the faith, taught him, and taken him along on his travels for years, the way a father would teach a son his trade. ‘True’ means genuine, the real thing. Timothy was Paul's son in every way that counted.

And the greeting has three words, not Paul's usual two. ‘Grace, mercy, and peace.’ Mercy is God's kindness to those who are weak or in trouble. It is the word Paul will use of himself in verses 13 and 16. A young man facing a hard task needed all three.
passages.ot:
God as Saviour runs through the Old Testament: “I, yes I, am the LORD, and there is no Savior but Me” (Isaiah 43:11). Paul calls God ‘our Savior’, and Christ Jesus ‘our hope’.

Grace, mercy and peace gather up the old blessing of Israel's priests: “May the LORD bless you and keep you” (Numbers 6:24), ending, “may the LORD lift up His countenance toward you and give you peace” (Numbers 6:26). And God's mercy is how he named himself to Moses: “The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6).
passages.asks: Paul calls Timothy his true child in the faith. Ask who has been that kind of father or mother in the faith to you, and whether you have thanked them. Ask whether there is someone younger you could help along in the same way. And ask which you need most today: grace, mercy, or peace.

passages.t: Stay in Ephesus: the goal is love
passages.happening:
“As I urged you on my departure to Macedonia, you should stay on at Ephesus to instruct certain men not to teach false doctrines or devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies, which promote speculation rather than the stewardship of God’s work, which is by faith” (verses 3-4).

“The goal of our instruction is the love that comes from a pure heart, a clear conscience, and a sincere faith. Some have strayed from these ways and turned aside to empty talk. They want to be teachers of the law, but they do not understand what they are saying or that which they so confidently assert” (verses 5-7).
passages.hearers:
Paul had left Ephesus for Macedonia, in northern Greece, and asked Timothy to stay behind. Acts does not tell of this trip, which is one reason many think it happened after the end of Acts.

The trouble was inside the church. ‘Certain men’ were teaching something different. Paul does not name the teaching in full, but he says what it looked like: ‘myths and endless genealogies’. Many think these were long stories spun out of the family lists and figures of the Old Testament, the kind of thing that can be argued about for ever. Paul says such talk only produces ‘speculation’, more questions, more quarrels.

Against it he sets ‘the stewardship of God's work’. The word means managing a household. God is running his household, the work of saving people, and people come into it ‘by faith’, not by clever theories.

Then verse 5, one of the most important in the letter. What is all teaching for? Not for winning arguments or sounding wise. ‘The goal of our instruction is the love that comes from a pure heart, a clear conscience, and a sincere faith.’ If teaching does not make people more loving, cleaner in heart and more honest in faith, it has missed the point.

The false teachers wanted to be ‘teachers of the law’. They were confident. But Paul says they did not understand what they were talking about. Confidence is not the same as knowledge.
passages.ot:
The Old Testament warns against prying into what God has not revealed: “The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things revealed belong to us and to our children forever, so that we may follow all the words of this law” (Deuteronomy 29:29). Notice the purpose: what God reveals is for living, not for speculation.

The Teacher of Ecclesiastes knew the weariness of endless argument: “There is no end to the making of many books, and much study wearies the body” (Ecclesiastes 12:12).

And the goal of love is the law's own goal: “love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18). A pure heart is what the Psalms ask for: “Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Psalm 51:10).
passages.asks: Paul says the goal of all teaching is love from a pure heart, a clear conscience and sincere faith. Ask whether what you read and hear about God is making you more loving, or only more argumentative. Ask whether there are questions you keep chasing that do not help you love God or anyone else. And ask whether your confidence about the Bible matches your understanding of it.

passages.t: The law is good, if used rightly
passages.happening:
“Now we know that the law is good, if one uses it legitimately” (verse 8).

“We realize that law is not enacted for the righteous, but for the lawless and rebellious, for the ungodly and sinful, for the unholy and profane, for killers of father or mother, for murderers, for the sexually immoral, for homosexuals, for slave traders and liars and perjurers, and for anyone else who is averse to sound teaching that agrees with the glorious gospel of the blessed God, with which I have been entrusted” (verses 9-11).
passages.hearers:
The false teachers wanted to be teachers of the law. Paul does not say the law is bad. He says the opposite: ‘the law is good’. But it must be used for what it is for.

What is it for? To show up wrong, so that people can see it. The law is like a mirror held up to the ‘lawless and rebellious’. It is not a book of puzzles for clever teachers to argue over.

The list that follows is long and blunt. Many readers notice that, after the first general words, it follows the order of the second half of the Ten Commandments. ‘Killers of father or mother’ break the command to honour parents. ‘Murderers’ break the command not to murder. ‘The sexually immoral’ and the next word stand for the command against adultery. ‘Slave traders’ break the command not to steal, for in the ancient world slave traders often kidnapped people to sell them. ‘Liars and perjurers’ break the command not to bear false witness. A Jewish reader would have heard the Ten Commandments behind it.

Then Paul says what all these have in common: they are opposed to ‘sound teaching’. ‘Sound’ means healthy. And sound teaching is the teaching that agrees with ‘the glorious gospel’ of God. The law exposes the disease. The gospel is the cure.
passages.ot:
The Psalms praise the law: “The Law of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul” (Psalm 19:7).

The commands behind the list are in Exodus 20: “Honor your father and mother”, “You shall not murder”, “You shall not commit adultery”, “You shall not steal”, “You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor” (Exodus 20:12-16).

The law treated kidnapping a person as one of the gravest crimes: “Whoever kidnaps another man must be put to death, whether he sells him or the man is found in his possession” (Exodus 21:16).

And the word the BSB renders ‘homosexuals’ seems to be built from the Greek words of the old Greek translation of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13, which forbid a man lying with a male.
passages.hard:
What does Paul say in verses 9 and 10, and how do Christians read the word the BSB renders ‘homosexuals’?

Paul gives a list of those for whom the law is meant: the lawless and rebellious, the ungodly, those who kill their parents, murderers, the sexually immoral, ‘homosexuals’, slave traders, liars and perjurers. These notes state that plainly and do not soften it.

The word the BSB renders ‘homosexuals’ is arsenokoitai. It is rare. In the New Testament it appears only here and in 1 Corinthians 6:9, and no clear use of it before Paul is known. It joins the Greek words for ‘male’ and ‘bed’.

Christians read it in more than one way. The historic reading of the church, and still the reading of most churches today, is that Paul speaks of same-sex sexual acts as such. On this reading the word points back to the law of Leviticus, which speaks of any man lying with a male, and Paul's teaching rests on God's creation of humanity as male and female (Genesis 1:27). Some Christians read it differently. They hold that the word points to particular practices of Paul's world, which they see as marked by exploitation, such as men's sexual use of boys, of slaves or of prostitutes, so that Paul was not speaking of faithful, committed same-sex relationships. Those who hold the historic reading answer that the law of Leviticus is general, and that Paul grounds sexual ethics in creation, not in particular abuses. These notes set out both readings. Faithful Christians disagree here, and these notes take no side. The site's note on 1 Corinthians 6:9-11 says more.

Three things are plain on any reading. First, the list also names murderers, slave traders, liars and perjurers, so that no reader stands outside it. Second, Paul's very next words are grace: “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the worst” (verse 15). The church is a company of the forgiven, not of the flawless. Third, nothing here gives anyone a reason for contempt toward any person.

If you are gay, or love someone who is, you are met with respect here. If these verses weigh on you, talk with a trusted pastor or friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul says the law is good when it is used rightly: to show us our wrong and send us to the gospel. Ask whether you use God's commands mostly on other people, or on yourself. Ask which line of the list would name you, and remember that verse 15 is for you too. And ask whether your teaching, or your talk about others, is healthy, the kind that makes people well.

passages.t: The worst of sinners, shown mercy
passages.happening:
“I thank Christ Jesus our Lord, who has strengthened me, that He considered me faithful and appointed me to service. I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and a violent man; yet because I had acted in ignorance and unbelief, I was shown mercy” (verses 12-13).

“This is a trustworthy saying, worthy of full acceptance: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the worst. But for this very reason I was shown mercy, so that in me, the worst of sinners, Christ Jesus might display His perfect patience as an example to those who would believe in Him for eternal life” (verses 15-16).

“Now to the King eternal, immortal, and invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
Right after the list of lawbreakers, Paul puts himself on it. He had been a ‘blasphemer’, speaking against Christ; a ‘persecutor’, hunting down believers; and ‘a violent man’, one who treated people with violence and contempt. Acts tells how he dragged believers off to prison (Acts 8:3). Paul does not stand outside the list and point. He stands in it.

And then the turn: ‘I was shown mercy’. The verb is passive. Paul did nothing to get it. Mercy was done to him.

Verse 15 is the first of the letter's ‘trustworthy sayings’, probably a well-known summary of the faith that Paul quotes and stands behind. It is the gospel in one line: ‘Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners.’ And Paul adds, ‘of whom I am the worst’. Not ‘I was’. ‘I am’. Years into his life as an apostle, he still sees himself as the clearest case of what grace can do.

That is why he was shown mercy: so that Christ could show his ‘perfect patience’ in him, as an example. If Christ could save the man who tried to destroy his church, he can save anyone. Paul is a display case of mercy.

And the passage ends in praise. When Paul thinks of mercy, he cannot help giving glory to God: the King who lives for ever, who cannot die, whom no one can see.
passages.ot:
God has always offered mercy to the worst: “Though your sins are like scarlet, they will be as white as snow” (Isaiah 1:18). “He has not dealt with us according to our sins or repaid us according to our iniquities” (Psalm 103:10).

David, a forgiven sinner, promised to do what Paul did with his story: “Then I will teach transgressors Your ways, and sinners will return to You” (Psalm 51:13).

And the King eternal is the God of the Psalms: “Your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and Your dominion endures through all generations” (Psalm 145:13). “from everlasting to everlasting You are God” (Psalm 90:2).
passages.asks: Paul calls himself the worst of sinners, and the clearest example of Christ's patience. Ask whether you think there is anyone too far gone for God's mercy, including yourself. Ask whether you tell your own story as Paul did, as a story of mercy. And ask when you last stopped, as Paul does here, simply to give God glory.

passages.t: Fight the good fight; do not shipwreck your faith
passages.happening:
“Timothy, my child, I entrust you with this command in keeping with the previous prophecies about you, so that by them you may fight the good fight, holding on to faith and a good conscience, which some have rejected and thereby shipwrecked their faith” (verses 18-19).

“Among them are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have handed over to Satan to be taught not to blaspheme” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
Paul hands Timothy a charge, like an officer giving an order. Earlier, it seems, people had spoken words over Timothy that they believed came from God, about the work he would do (see 4:14). Paul tells him to remember them when the fight gets hard.

The ‘good fight’ is a soldier's picture. Then Paul changes the picture to the sea. Some have ‘shipwrecked their faith’. They threw away a ‘good conscience’, the inner sense of right and wrong, and once the hull was gone, their faith ran aground. For Paul, what you believe and how you live are never separate. Ignore your conscience long enough and your faith will not survive.

Two men are named. Hymenaeus appears again in 2 Timothy 2:17-18, teaching that the resurrection had already happened. An Alexander who did Paul great harm appears in 2 Timothy 4:14, though it is not certain he is the same man; the name was common.

Paul says he ‘handed them over to Satan’. He uses the same words in 1 Corinthians 5:5. Most readers take it to mean putting them out of the church's fellowship, back into the world where Satan's power is at work. But notice the purpose: ‘to be taught not to blaspheme’. The aim is that they learn, and come back.
passages.ot:
The life of faith as a fight runs through the Old Testament: “Be strong and courageous” (Psalm 31:24).

The heart, which Paul calls the conscience, must be guarded: “Guard your heart with all diligence, for from it flow springs of life” (Proverbs 4:23).

And the way back for anyone who has gone wrong is confession: “Then I acknowledged my sin to You and did not hide my iniquity”, and “You forgave the guilt of my sin” (Psalm 32:5).
passages.hard:
What does ‘handed over to Satan’ mean, and how should churches use discipline?

The phrase is hard, and it should not be made to sound easy. Most readers take it to mean that Paul put these two men out of the church's fellowship, back into the world, which the New Testament sees as the realm where Satan has power. Some think it also meant suffering in body, though the text does not say so. On every reading the purpose is plain in the verse itself: ‘to be taught not to blaspheme’. The aim is correction, not destruction. And these were teachers who were leading others away from the faith.

Churches have answered in different ways. Some can keep a person from Communion for a time, hoping to bring them back. Some practise church discipline carried out by elders, and some by the whole congregation. Others use little formal discipline and rely on pastoral care. These notes do not choose among the churches' practices.

This passage has also been badly misused, and that must be faced. Church discipline must never be used to silence someone who has been harmed, to protect someone who has done harm, or to punish someone for asking questions or telling the truth. Abuse and other crimes are reported to the police and the proper authorities, whom Paul calls “God’s servant, an agent of retribution to the wrongdoer” (Romans 13:4). A church meeting is never a substitute for that.

A word to anyone who has been hurt by a church's discipline, or shunned by a church or a family. What happened to you may have been wrong, and it is not wrong to grieve it. Paul's goal was always restoration and comfort, never cruelty or contempt. “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted” (Psalm 34:18). If this still weighs on you, please talk with someone you trust, a pastor, a friend or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul says that rejecting a good conscience can shipwreck faith. Ask whether there is something your conscience keeps telling you that you keep ignoring. Ask what words of encouragement God has given you that you need to remember in a hard fight. And ask whether there is someone who has drifted whom you could still try to win back.
